person.name: Zaha_Hadid
person.summary: Zaha Hadid was an Iraqi-British architect, designer, and artist whose radical, fluid geometries transformed late‑20th and early‑21st‑century architecture. Trained in mathematics in Beirut and architecture in London, she first gained fame for visionary, often unbuilt projects before emerging as a global practitioner with landmark works such as the Vitra Fire Station, Bergisel Ski Jump, MAXXI, Guangzhou Opera House, and the London Aquatics Centre. In 2004 she became the first woman to receive the Pritzker Architecture Prize and later won consecutive Stirling Prizes, a Damehood, and the RIBA Royal Gold Medal. She died in 2016 with numerous major projects still under construction worldwide.

chapters.headline: Cosmopolitan Formative Years
chapters.description: Early life in Iraq and Europe shapes her cosmopolitan outlook and awakens a fascination with architecture and abstraction.

chapters.headline: Avant‑Garde Education Experimentation
chapters.description: Intense architectural training in London and early professional work in Europe establish her radical design language and reputation within avant‑garde circles.

chapters.headline: From Paper to Built Forms
chapters.description: Her transition from visionary unbuilt projects to realized buildings begins, as early commissions in Europe prove her radical architecture can be constructed.

chapters.headline: Global Acclaim Ascendant
chapters.description: Major cultural projects, landmark awards, and expanding international commissions cement her status as a leading global architect.

chapters.headline: Late Honours Enduring Legacy
chapters.description: Prestigious British honours, Olympic visibility, and final awards precede her sudden death, leaving a thriving global practice and ongoing projects as her legacy.

events.title: Birth in Baghdad
events.description: Zaha Mohammad Hadid is born into an upper‑class Iraqi family in Baghdad. Her father, Muhammad al‑Hajj Husayn Hadid, is an industrialist and prominent democratic politician, and her mother, Wajiha al‑Sabunji, is an artist. Growing up in a cosmopolitan, politically engaged household with roots in Mosul exposes her early to both modernity and the cultural depth of the region.

events.date_note: Represents her childhood and teenage years in the early–mid 1960s
events.title: Early inspirations and schooling
events.description: As a child and teenager, Hadid travels with her family to ancient Sumerian cities in southern Iraq, an experience she later credits with sparking her fascination with architecture and landscape. During the 1960s she attends boarding schools in England and Switzerland, gaining fluency in multiple cultures and languages. This mix of Mesopotamian heritage and European education shapes her later ability to work confidently across continents.

events.date_note: Approximate year she completes undergraduate study
events.title: Studies mathematics in Beirut
events.description: Hadid studies mathematics at the American University of Beirut, immersing herself in a rigorous, abstract discipline before turning formally to architecture. The training in mathematical thinking later underpins her willingness to engage with advanced geometry and complex structural forms. Beirut at this time is a lively intellectual and cultural centre, reinforcing her cosmopolitan outlook.

events.title: Enrolls at AA School, London
events.description: Hadid moves to London and enrolls at the Architectural Association School of Architecture, then one of the most radical architecture schools in Europe. She studies under figures such as Rem Koolhaas, Elia Zenghelis and Bernard Tschumi, who recognize her as an exceptionally original talent. Within the AA's experimental milieu she begins to push beyond conventional drawing, developing abstract paintings as a primary design tool.

events.title: Thesis 'Malevich's Tektonik' and joins OMA
events.description: Hadid completes her AA graduation thesis, 'Malevich's [[Suprematism|Tektonik]]', a visionary design for a multi‑level hotel on London's Hungerford Bridge, rendered as a large acrylic painting influenced by Suprematism and Kazimir Malevich. The project crystallizes her interest in abstraction, fragmentation and dynamic urban form. After graduating she joins her former teachers Rem Koolhaas and Elia Zenghelis at the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA) in Rotterdam, gaining early experience in avant‑garde practice.

Suprematism.explanation: Suprematism is an early 20th‑century avant‑garde art movement, founded by Kazimir Malevich in Russia, focused on basic geometric forms and pure artistic feeling rather than depicting objects.

events.date_note: Around this time she also becomes a naturalised citizen of the United Kingdom
events.title: Founds Zaha Hadid Architects
events.description: Hadid establishes her own practice, Zaha Hadid Architects, in London, marking the start of her career as an independent architect. At a moment when postmodern historicism dominates, she pursues an uncompromisingly experimental modernism, expressed through highly detailed paintings and drawings. In parallel she begins a long teaching career at the Architectural Association and later at Harvard, Cambridge, Chicago, Hamburg, Illinois at Chicago, and Columbia, spreading her ideas through studios and lectures worldwide.

images.caption: The former Bowling Green Lane School in Clerkenwell, London. The building is now the studio of Zaha Hadid Architects, the practice founded the late architect Zaha Hadid.

events.title: Wins The Peak competition
events.description: Hadid wins the international competition for The Peak, a leisure club carved into a Hong Kong hillside, with a daring, fractured composition that seems to explode the mountain. Though never built, the project’s drawings and paintings become icons of radical late‑20th‑century architecture. Throughout the 1980s she gains a reputation as a 'paper architect' whose unbuilt schemes, such as The Peak and a later Cardiff Bay opera house proposal, profoundly influence discourse despite remaining unrealized.

events.title: MoMA Deconstructivism breakthrough
events.description: Her work is featured in the landmark '[[Deconstructivist Architecture|Deconstructivist Architecture]]' exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, curated by Philip Johnson and Mark Wigley. Shown alongside architects such as Frank Gehry and Rem Koolhaas, Hadid is identified as a key figure in a new, formally adventurous strain of architecture. The exhibition and related conferences at institutions including the Tate in London propel her name onto the global architectural stage.

Deconstructivist Architecture.explanation: 'Deconstructivist Architecture' was a 1988 exhibition at New York's Museum of Modern Art that introduced and grouped several architects under the emerging style later known as deconstructivism, helping to define a major late-20th-century architectural movement.

events.title: Vitra Fire Station completed
events.description: The Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein, commissioned by Vitra director Rolf Fehlbaum, becomes Hadid’s first major built work. Constructed from raw concrete and glass with sharp, colliding planes, the building reads as a frozen snapshot of movement rather than a conventional fire station. Although it soon becomes an exhibition space rather than a working station, the project serves as the launching pad of her built career and demonstrates that her radical language can be realized in concrete and steel.

images.caption: Vitra Feuerwehrhaus von Zaha Hadid in Weil am Rhein

events.title: Bergisel Ski Jump opens
events.description: Hadid’s Bergisel Ski Jump in Innsbruck is completed, replacing an older Olympic structure with a striking 'organic hybrid' that fuses tower, bridge, and viewing platform. Built under tight time pressure and amid resistance from traditionalists, the 48‑metre‑high concrete and steel form showcases her ability to translate dynamic movement into built form. The project leads to a series of European commissions, including housing in Berlin and the Spittelau Viaducts housing scheme in Vienna.

images.caption: View of Bergisel ski jumping hill in Innsbruck (Austria) from the South

events.title: Contemporary Arts Center Cincinnati
events.description: The Contemporary Arts Center in Cincinnati opens, making Hadid the first woman to design a major art museum in the United States. The building’s dramatic interior, organized around a 30‑metre black stairway slicing between curving concrete walls, demonstrates how her abstract formal language can create powerful public spaces. Around the same period she wins and executes further large commissions such as the Phaeno Science Center in Wolfsburg and the BMW administration building in Leipzig, consolidating her global presence.

images.caption: The Contemporary Art Center, Cincinnati OH by: Zaha Hadid.

events.title: Awarded Pritzker Architecture Prize
events.description: Hadid receives the [[Pritzker Architecture Prize|Pritzker Architecture Prize]], becoming the first woman to be honoured with what is often called the 'Nobel Prize of architecture'. The award recognizes both her visionary unbuilt work and her emerging portfolio of completed projects across Europe and North America. It significantly increases her visibility and leads to a surge of high‑profile commissions, including museums, cultural centres, and urban masterplans from Guangzhou to Rome.

Pritzker Architecture Prize.explanation: An international architecture award established in 1979 and funded by the Pritzker family, widely regarded as the most prestigious prize in architecture.

events.date_note: Spans consecutive Stirling Prize awards in 2010 and 2011
events.title: Back‑to‑back Stirling Prizes
events.description: Hadid wins the UK’s Stirling Prize in 2010 for [[MAXXI|MAXXI, the National Museum of 21st Century Arts]] in Rome, whose flowing concrete galleries and bridges embody her fluid spatial language. In 2011 she receives the prize again, this time for the Evelyn Grace Academy in London, a school organized around a dynamic, zigzagging running track. The consecutive awards confirm her practice as one of the most influential and consistently celebrated of its generation.

images.caption: L'entrée du musée conçu par l'architecte Zaha Hadid Le Musée national des arts du XXI siècle (MAXXI) est une Fondation créée par le Ministère italien de la culture. C'est la première institution nationale italienne dédiée à la création contemporaine : aux arts et à l'architecture. Elle donne à Rome l'espace dédié à l'art contemporain qui lui manquait. Le MAXXI est un lieu de conservation et d’exposition mais également un laboratoire d’expérimentation et d’innovation culturelle, d’étude, de recherche et de production de contenus esthétiques d'aujourd'hui. Le bâtiment (terrain : 29.000 m2, intérieur bâti 21.000 m2, extérieur 19.640 m2, espaces d'exposition : 10.000 m2, services : 6.200 m2) qui abrite le MAXXI a été conçu par l'architecte anglo-irakienne Zaha Hadid [1950-2016]. Zaha Hadid était l'une des architectes contemporaines les plus créatrices, voir son site : www.zaha-hadid.com/cultural/maxxi Le MAXXI est situé dans le quartier populaire de Flaminio au nord de Rome, à proximité du palais de la musique conçu par Renzo Piano et d'équipements sportifs importants. Le MAXXI a été inauguré le 1er juin 2010. Il s'agit d'une oeuvre architecturale très innovante, très bien intégrée à l'environnement urbain (le bâtiment est à la hauteur des maisons existantes), qui privilégie les visiteurs plus que les oeuvres (les cimaises apparaissent complexes à utiliser) à travers sa conception ouverte des espaces d'exposition et de circulation tant sur l'intérieur du bâtiment que sur son contexte urbain. C'est un élément marquant de sa conception. La grande innovation technique pour la construction du MAXXI réside, selon l'architecte, dans la fabrication des murs (souvent très longs) qui ont été coulés sur place dans un béton auto-compactant. Le bâtiment s'étend sur 3 niveaux et comporte 5 galeries d'exposition qui communiquent entre elles et qui sont visuellement ouvertes les unes sur les autres. Les visiteurs circulent à travers des passerelles très longues permettant de voir les salles mais également l'extérieur. Ces passerelles très allongées qui s'entremêlent donnent un caractère singulier à ce bâtiment et ne lui font ressembler à aucun autre. Dans les salles, peu de murs sont verticaux ce qui n'est guère commode pour exposer des oeuvres mais à ce sujet d'autres exemples existent comme le musée de Bilbao conçu par F.O. Gehry. La création architecturale semble presque prendre le pas sur le contenu artistique des collections mais c'est une tendance générale dans le monde des musées créés récemment. Site du Musée national des arts du 21ème siècle (MAXXI, Rome) www.fondazionemaxxi.it/en/

MAXXI.explanation: The National Museum of 21st Century Arts in Rome, a state-run contemporary art and architecture museum designed by Zaha Hadid and completed in 2010.

events.title: London Aquatics Centre and Damehood
events.description: Her [[London Aquatics Centre|London Aquatics Centre]], with its sweeping wave‑like roof, serves as a centerpiece of the 2012 Olympic Games and introduces her work to a vast global television audience. The building’s transformation from Olympic venue to community facility demonstrates her interest in long‑term urban legacy. The same year Queen Elizabeth II appoints her Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire for services to architecture, formal recognition of her impact on British and international design.

images.caption: London Aquatics Centre was the venue for swimming, diving and synchronised swimming events during the London 2012 Summer Olympics and Summer Para Olympics Games, 2016 European Aquatics Championships. Architect -Zaha Hadid Architect Completion - 2011 https://www.zaha-hadid.com/architecture/london-aquatics-centre/

London Aquatics Centre.explanation: An indoor swimming and diving facility in the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in London, designed by Zaha Hadid as one of the main venues for the 2012 Summer Olympics and later converted for public and community use.

events.date_note: Month of the Royal Gold Medal presentation; exact day not specified
events.title: Receives RIBA Royal Gold Medal
events.description: In one of her final public honours, Hadid is awarded the Royal Gold Medal by the [[Royal Institute of British Architects|Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA)]], becoming the first woman to receive the medal in her own right. The award, personally approved by Queen Elizabeth II, recognizes a lifetime of achievements that reshaped architectural geometry and expanded the possibilities of digital design and engineering. By this point her office is overseeing major projects worldwide, including airports, museums and stadiums still under construction.

Royal Institute of British Architects.explanation: The Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) is the main professional body for architects in the United Kingdom, which awards the Royal Gold Medal in recognition of a lifetime’s work in architecture.

events.title: Death in Miami
events.description: Hadid dies suddenly in [[Miami|Miami]], after suffering a heart attack while being treated for bronchitis, cutting short a career still in full momentum. She leaves behind no spouse or children but a large extended family and a global practice led by longtime collaborator Patrik Schumacher. At the time of her death many of her most ambitious projects, including major transport hubs and sports venues, are still in progress, ensuring that her built legacy will continue to expand posthumously.

Miami.explanation: Major city in southeastern Florida that serves as an international center for finance, culture, and tourism; Zaha Hadid died there in 2016 while visiting.
